messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At sixty-three, Rania had spent her adult life as a solitary auditor, but a single afternoon in a desert canyon had permanently fractured her sense of security. Three years ago, while hiking with her younger brother, a sudden monsoon had swollen a dry wash into a violent current. They had scrambled into a ranger’s maintenance shed, but the heavy steel door had slammed shut and the rusted latch had fused. In that locked space, the water rose, the temperature plummeted, and the natural world outside became a relentless, inescapable pressure against the walls. When they finally forced the door with a rock, her brother was already gone. The trauma had not been in the open trail, but in that confined darkness where nature offered no exit and the victim’s face had been the last thing she saw. This exact confluence of trapped confinement and wild terrain made the landscape itself a direct conduit to the event, ensuring that any similar setting would immediately bridge past and present. When the original triggers surfaced, they directly summoned the full sensory reliving of the canyon, flooding her with the exact terror she felt at the time. She would describe the flashbacks by saying the water and darkness filled her mouth and lungs exactly as they had that night, proving to her that her body was an enemy reacting to phantom danger. These intrusive memories immediately amplified her sense of threat, pushing her to avoid going to unfamiliar places because she could no longer assess the danger. Her conviction that she was powerless to stop bad things from happening, alongside her belief that her body was betraying her, directly fed the flashbacks; when she felt helpless, her mind would seize upon the locked-room memory to prove the world was inherently unsafe. Her loss of faith also made the original triggers feel more potent, as she could no longer dismiss the canyon or the locked cabin as mere history. The sheer weight of those confined rooms and wild terrain convinced her she had lost faith in life and higher powers, cementing her conviction that tragedy was inevitable. The chronic sleep deprivation and hypervigilance she maintained at work eroded her remaining trust in her own mind, solidifying her helplessness and loss of faith. The constant state of alarm made the original triggers feel overwhelmingly intrusive, forcing her to retreat from any setting that resembled a locked space or natural environment. Occasionally, the memory itself would spark a faint urge to check her surroundings, though that was a fleeting slip. The cycle tightened over the last eighteen months until her daily life narrowed to familiar perimeters. During a routine audit at a remote municipal building, she found herself unable to navigate the unfamiliar corridors, which forced her to request a permanent desk assignment in the familiar headquarters. This occupational limitation cemented her belief that she was fundamentally unsafe, which directly drove her threat responses, keeping her hypervigilant and unable to sleep even in her quiet apartment. When a locked elevator caught her between floors during an inspection, the full sensory reliving of the flood overwhelmed her completely, triggering the panic attacks that finally broke her routine. She realized she could no longer outrun the episodes, nor could she trust her own nervous system to distinguish past from present. The terror on recall and the triggered without warning symptoms bled into her daily routine, ensuring that every unfamiliar place felt like a tomb. Her helplessness and loss of faith solidified her avoidance of new environments, while her hypervigilance and sleep problems confirmed her worst fears about her body, creating a loop that felt both inescapable and logical. The original triggers continued to feed her negative beliefs, while her negative appraisals kept her hyperaware of every potential danger, ensuring that the memory would always return with full sensory intensity. Rania finally walked into the clinic because her close colleague had quietly arranged her leave, telling her she was disappearing, and because the sheer exhaustion of maintaining two lives was tearing her apart. She was most afraid that she would never feel safe in her own skin again, but what she hoped for, more than anything, was to wake up without bracing for a door that would never open.
